Pregnancy

9 to 12 Weeks Pregnant: Symptoms, Screening, Baby Growth

Updated: August 26, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

At 12 weeks pregnant, your baby measures about 5 to 6 cm from crown to rump, roughly the size of a lime, and every major organ has formed and is now busy growing. The stretch from week 9 to week 12 also covers the official shift from embryo to fetus, the usual peak of nausea, and the first big screening decisions, with NIPT possible from 10 weeks and the nuchal translucency scan at about 11 to 13 weeks. Here is what is happening, how you might feel, and what is worth doing before these windows close.

From embryo to fetus: what changes in weeks 9 to 12

Around week 10, your baby graduates from embryo to fetus. The new name marks a real milestone: every major organ and body system has formed, and the work from here is growth and maturing rather than building from scratch. The size change across these weeks is striking. At week 9, your baby is about the size of a grape. By week 12, the crown to rump measurement is roughly 5 to 6 cm, about the size of a lime. The head still looks large compared with the body, which is normal at this stage, and the proportions slowly even out over the months ahead.

A lot is happening in the details. Fingers and toes have separated, and tiny nails are starting to form. The intestines, which developed partly inside the umbilical cord, are moving into the abdomen. The kidneys begin producing urine, and the baby swallows small amounts of amniotic fluid. There is real movement too: stretching, flexing, even hiccup-like motions, although the baby is far too small for you to feel any of it yet. Near the end of this stretch, the placenta takes over most hormone production from the ovary, one reason many early symptoms begin to ease as you approach the second trimester.

How you might feel right now

For many people, nausea peaks somewhere around weeks 9 to 10 and then slowly loosens its grip between weeks 12 and 14. That timing is an average, not a promise. Some feel better sooner, some carry queasiness into the second trimester, and some never had it at all, which is also normal. Fatigue can be heavy through these weeks, the kind that makes an early bedtime feel non-negotiable. Food aversions and a sharp sense of smell are common, and bloating can make your waistband tight long before there is a true bump. If you want practical relief ideas, our guide to easing pregnancy nausea covers them in depth.

You may also notice sore breasts, more saliva than usual, constipation, mild headaches, and mood swings that arrive without warning. Hormone levels are still climbing, and carrying a big secret while feeling unwell is genuinely tiring, so be patient with yourself. One quiet worry deserves a mention: some people panic when symptoms fade around week 11 or 12, but easing nausea at this stage usually reflects the normal hormonal shift, not a problem. Symptoms are a rough signal at best. If something feels wrong to you, or if vomiting is so constant that fluids will not stay down, contact your clinic rather than waiting it out.

Screening decisions: NIPT and the nuchal scan

Weeks 9 to 12 open the main first-trimester screening window, and the timing matters. Cell-free DNA screening, usually called NIPT, is a blood draw available from 10 weeks onward that screens for the most common chromosomal conditions. The nuchal translucency scan, an ultrasound that measures fluid at the back of the baby's neck, is done at about 11 to 13 weeks and is often combined with blood work as first-trimester combined screening. These are screening tests: they estimate chance, they do not give a diagnosis. What each test measures and how to read the results are covered in our guide to pregnancy blood tests and screening.

Screening is a choice, not a requirement. Some people want as much information as early as possible, others prefer to skip optional tests, and both are reasonable. It helps to decide before the window arrives, because the nuchal scan cannot be done accurately after about 13 to 14 weeks. Useful questions for your clinic: which screens do you offer, what do they cost or does insurance cover them, how long do results take, and what would the next step be after a higher-chance result. Talk it through with your partner or a support person if the decision feels heavy. There is no single right answer, only the one that fits you.

Hearing the heartbeat

At a prenatal visit, a handheld doppler can often pick up the heartbeat somewhere around 10 to 12 weeks. Often is the honest word. Whether it works at a given visit depends on the position of the uterus and placenta, your body build, and how far along you actually are, since dating can be off by several days. Not finding the heartbeat with a doppler at this stage is common and is not, by itself, a sign that something is wrong. When a clinician cannot find it and wants reassurance, an ultrasound gives a much clearer answer, and many clinics move straight to one rather than searching for long.

Home dopplers deserve a careful word. They are easy to buy and hard to use well. Untrained ears often mistake the mother's own pulse or blood flow through the placenta for the baby's heartbeat, which can give false reassurance when something needs attention, or false alarm when everything is fine. Most maternity guidance suggests leaving doppler checks to trained clinicians for exactly this reason. If you are worried between appointments, especially about bleeding, pain, or a sudden change in how you feel, call your clinic and describe the symptoms. A short phone conversation with someone qualified is worth more than an hour of anxious searching with a device at home.

Your to-do list, and when to call

A few tasks are genuinely time-sensitive right now. If you want the nuchal translucency scan, book it early, because the measurement window closes at about 13 to 14 weeks and appointment slots fill. Decide whether you want NIPT, and if so, arrange the blood draw any time from 10 weeks. If you have not had a first prenatal visit, schedule one. This is also when many people plan how to share the news. Waiting until after 12 weeks or the first scan is common, but there is no rule; a good test is to tell the people you would want support from if anything changed. Jot dates, symptoms, and questions in BeMama or a notebook so nothing gets lost.

Some symptoms need a same-day call to your clinic, whatever the hour: bleeding heavier than light spotting, cramping that keeps getting worse, a fever of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, or burning when you urinate. So does vomiting that will not let fluids stay down, especially with signs of dehydration like dark urine or lightheadedness, since treatment can help and nobody should simply endure it. A smaller set of symptoms means emergency care right away rather than waiting for a callback: severe or one-sided belly pain, pain with dizziness, fainting, or shoulder-tip pain, or bleeding that soaks a pad within an hour, because these can signal internal bleeding that must be checked immediately. Light spotting on its own is common in early pregnancy and often harmless, but mention it at your next visit; when you are unsure which category you are in, call, because triage nurses answer exactly these questions all day.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pregnancy is dated from the first day of the last menstrual period and is commonly described in weeks and trimesters. ACOG’s week ranges describe typical development, but they are an orientation rather than a test of an individual fetus.

Due dates are estimates, and ultrasound is used for medical reasons to assess gestational age, growth, anatomy, position, and other questions. Only a qualified prenatal professional can interpret findings for a specific pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama’s week view for education, appointment preparation, and dated notes. It cannot confirm fetal growth, anatomy, heartbeat, or wellbeing.

When to seek help

Contact your prenatal team for bleeding, severe pain, fluid leakage, reduced movement after movement is established, or any urgent concern instead of relying on a week-by-week article.

Evidence notes updated: August 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Around week 10 your baby officially becomes a fetus, and by week 12 measures about 5 to 6 cm, the size of a lime.
  • Nausea often peaks near weeks 9 to 10 and eases for many people between weeks 12 and 14.
  • NIPT is possible from 10 weeks, and the nuchal translucency scan happens at about 11 to 13 weeks.
  • A doppler often finds the heartbeat around 10 to 12 weeks, but not always, and that alone is not alarming.
  • Call your clinic the same day for heavy bleeding, worsening cramps, fever, or vomiting that keeps fluids from staying down; severe one-sided pain with dizziness or shoulder pain means emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

When can you get NIPT testing?

NIPT, the cell-free DNA blood test, can be done any time from 10 weeks of pregnancy onward. There is no late cutoff, so you can also choose it after the first trimester if you decide later. It is a screening test that estimates the chance of common chromosomal conditions, not a diagnosis, so a higher-chance result would be followed by confirmatory testing.

When does morning sickness peak?

Nausea most often peaks around weeks 9 to 10 and starts easing between weeks 12 and 14. The pattern varies a lot from person to person, and some people stay queasy well into the second trimester. Contact your clinician if vomiting keeps you from holding down fluids, because effective treatment exists and you do not have to wait it out.

What week is the nuchal translucency scan done?

The nuchal translucency scan is done at about 11 to 13 weeks of pregnancy. The measurement is only accurate inside that window, so it helps to book early once your clinic offers it. It is often paired with a blood test as first-trimester combined screening, and like all screening it is optional.

When can you hear the heartbeat with a doppler?

A clinician can often find the heartbeat with a handheld doppler around 10 to 12 weeks, though sometimes not until a little later. The position of the uterus and placenta, body build, and dating that is off by a few days all affect it. Not hearing it at this stage is common and not by itself a warning sign; an ultrasound can confirm quickly if reassurance is needed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
